items.rationale: The difference is who owns the control flow: in a workflow, developer code sets the path (predefined code paths); in an agent, the model directs its own steps and tool use. Counting model calls (b) or the presence of tools (c) does not separate them, since workflows can make many calls and use tools, and human approval (d) is a separate design choice.

The model's label is only an input; the code decides which fixed path runs next, so this is a workflow (the routing pattern). Using a model to make a choice (a) or calling it more than once (b) does not make a system an agent; an agent chooses its own steps and tool use. Option d is wrong on its reasoning: workflows can use tools and search, so the absence of tools is not what makes this one a workflow.

Booking has known steps in a known order, which is what a fixed workflow suits: predictable and cheap. The other three are open-ended, with a number of steps and manual pages that cannot be predicted in advance, which is where an agent's flexibility pays off.

items.answer: When the steps are known in advance, code can run them predictably, faster and more cheaply, so the model's freedom to choose steps only adds cost, delay and error risk.
accepted: A fixed workflow is cheaper and more predictable because the steps are known, so an agent's flexibility is not needed.
Workflows cost less and are more predictable and reliable than agents when the task is well defined.
Agents add cost, latency and risk of errors that a fixed, known sequence does not need.
items.rationale: Full credit names a benefit of the workflow (lower cost or latency, predictability or reliability) and ties it to the steps being known or fixed. Saying only that workflows are simpler, or that agents are bad, is partial. Claiming agents are always better, or that workflows are more capable, shows M8.

Agents typically trade cost and latency for flexibility and task performance, so choose one only when the flexibility is needed, as it is when steps cannot be predicted. Equal cost (a) and always-better quality (b) ignore that trade; cheaper because of skipped steps (c) is backwards, since the agent loop adds model calls.

The agent's model is called once for the question and once for each of the 5 tool results: 1 + 5 = 6 calls. The workflow makes 3, so the agent makes 6 - 3 = 3 more. Answering 5 counts only the tool requests, and 2 or 8 come from miscounting the question or the final answer.
